story_text.value:
Daybot is ranked number two in Canada, after Shopify, for making e-commerce stores.

With a lot of AI-generated stores like Daybot's, we ran into the issue of the CSS sometimes not being up to standard. For example, the text and the background might end up the same color. I've also seen that race conditions often happen on the client side and are never caught in test cases, because they aren't tested under load, or because clients sometimes do actions that are just random.

With AI-generated code becoming more popular, we thought that an AI agent that runs in the browser at runtime, is very lightweight, catches bugs like race conditions, stops unintended behavior, and gets better the more users use it would completely change the game. Now you can even run code faster.

So I want you to try it out. You can add it with one line. It's published as an npm package. Please let me know what you think.

title.value: Show HN: GenClass, A 10 MB in-browser model that catches bugs that never throw

story_text.value:
Hi HN, excited to be open sourcing two tools that we have built over past few months which helps to understand your own work with AI coding agents

Agent Desk is a local macOS app which allows you to browse your sessions across all top coding agents - Claude code, cursor, codex, github copilot, Kiro, Antigravity. You can find sessions by your projects, revisit those conversations, understand and inspect your entire harness - rules, skills, hooks, subagents.

https://github.com/tetriz-ai/agent-desk

Session Intelligence is a go library which helps structure and analyse your session transcripts using your own LLM. It can help understand missing context, repeated corrections, if session reached its goal and where is effort being wasted. It can also surface leaked credentials and PII.

https://github.com/tetriz-ai/session-intelligence

Both are MIT-licensed.

You can also combine both together and understanding your agent steering habits better.

Excited about the community using it.

title.value: Show HN: Evaluate and improve your agent steering

story_text.value:
The AI Hub provides 91 curated lesson plans teaching middle and high school students about AI - how it works, what the risks and benefits of AI are, and how it is impacting society.

These activities come from six different nonprofit organizations that are building educational resources for classrooms. Our nonprofit worked with 16 different teachers to comb through more than 200 different resources, with the teachers vetting these resources to find the best resources for their classrooms. The end result is 91 different lesson plans and activities that cover a wide range of different topics.

Schools across Pittsburgh will be using these resources over the course of this year to help teach their students about AI, and they will be scaled up nationally over the coming years.

If you're a human that has thoughts or feedback, please drop a comment!

What's top of mind: "What else should we teach students?"

I'd appreciate any ideas you all have as we continue to build and refine this library of resources.

Coding agents kept filling up my disk with stale worktrees and leaving branches behind, so I built Fresh to clean up merged branches and worktrees and switch back to the default branch after merging a PR.

Now for all my projects, it’s just one action: fresh.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Niz. Pulse Local is a budgeting app for Mac (Apple Silicon, beta) that answers questions about your spending with models that run on your machine. Local mode needs no account. The ledger and your questions stay on the machine, and the app sends no analytics or crash logs.

I felt there are not enough consumer apps that run locally with no calls to the outside world that help us manage sensitive corners of our lives. This app in its local variant only downloads a couple of models and occasional updates, it does not send any analytics nor data.

Features-wise, Pulse local is a complete budgeting app that offers an assistant built on top of a fine-tuned model and thousands of rules embedded in the code itself. I'm sharing it for free with options to help me continue experimenting with fine-tuning and expanding along this direction.

How it works: you import a CSV from any bank, in any currency. When you ask a question, a tuned Qwen3 0.6B model reads it into a structured query, and code, not the model, does the money math against the ledger. A 4B checker model double-checks each money answer; when the two readings disagree, the app says it is not sure instead of guessing. That change took wrong answers from about one in five to 5 in 494 questions across our last three tests. The write-up covers how we test, the designs that failed, and the limits of the claim: https://pulseos.finance/pulse-local/writing/agree-or-not-sur...

The tuned weights are on Hugging Face (PulseOS/pulse-local-qwen3-0.6b).

Limitations: the first start downloads about 2.9 GB of models. With the checker on, a money answer takes 12 to 14 seconds (you can turn the checker off). Small models can still misread an open-ended question. The app answers in English. Mac only for now; Windows is next.

The app is free. An optional Connected mode (Sync Pass, $29/year) syncs US banks through Plaid; transactions pass through our server's memory and are not stored.

Feedback welcome, especially on wrong answers and on questions it should handle but does not.

title.value: Show HN: Pulse Local, a Mac budgeting app whose AI models run on your machine

Showing off Sugabots, an internal project I built at work that we've decided to open-source.

I got tired of the team just copying context between agents and Slack. So I built an internal tool for shared chats where our team and agents could work together, using our choice of models and tools.

The team is now actively maintaining and building on it to add all the features we're missing. We've shared a hosted offering with a few other teams and has proven useful for them too.

Its open-source (MIT) and self-hostable if you want to use it yourself.

Let me know what you think.

story_text.value:
The URL is to a public stack page. Without an account you can view the supplement catalog. It contains over 300 supplements. Yes it is AI generated but through a fairly long process that involves pulling the latest research, finding sources for supplement dosage and discovering contraindications, interactions and synergies between supplements.

If you're into taking health supplements, it's a great app. I made it for myself initially then just kept going with it, adding features that I wanted as I went along. Now it can even scan your supplement bottles for whats inside and it's pretty accurate. If you're using the phone app and know how to take a picture it will read your bottle correctly.

Open to honest feedback from people who actually use a lot of supplements. If you do make an account, it's free, no paid tier or even ads.

story_text.value:
Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects.

Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units.

GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked).

Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models.

GitHub: https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony

Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks.

title.value: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
